intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). Physics is the science of how things move, interact, and exist—from the tiniest particles inside atoms to the vast galaxies stretching across space. It’s the foundation of modern technology, the reason rockets fly, and the explanation behind everyday phenomena like why your phone works or how a soccer ball curves through the air.

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol rolls two solid spheres of the exact same size and shape down an inclined ramp from rest: one made of aluminum and one made of heavy brass. Neglecting air resistance, how do their accelerations down the ramp compare?
options: The heavier brass sphere accelerates twice as fast because it has more gravitational mass.
Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
The lighter aluminum sphere reaches the bottom first because it has less friction.
quiz_item.correct_answer: Option B — Both solid spheres accelerate at the same rate (a = 5/7 g sin theta) regardless of mass when shape and radius match.
quiz_item.explanation: Since both gravitational force and moment of inertia are proportional to mass (I = 2/5 m r^2), mass cancels out of the equation of motion on an incline.

requirements.req_text: Hands-On Experimentation. Conduct THREE physics experiments, selecting from the following options. Each experiment must include: a hypothesis, materials used, safety precautions, observations, and conclusions based on results. Explain how each experiment demonstrates key physics principles. For each experiment, be sure to try variations/variables to test your hypothesis. (A) Option A: Newton’s Laws in Action: Balloon-Powered Car. Make and test a balloon-powered car to show how force and motion interact. (B) Option B: Momentum: Stacked Ball Drop. Drop different-sized stacked balls to show momentum. (C) Option C: Centrifugal Force. Make spinning toys to demonstrate centrifugal force. (D) Option D: Centripetal Force. Swing a water bucket or tray filled with water glasses to demonstrate centripetal force. (E) Option E: Balance. Explore center of gravity, inertia, and harmonic motion using a Tweety Bopper. (F) Option F: Visualize Sound. Visualize Chladni patterns using a tonoscope. (G) Option G: Cartesian Diver. Demonstrate buoyancy and the ideal gas law with Cartesian divers. (H) Option H: Air Pressure: Bernoulli’s principle and the Coandă Effect. Balance different objects in a stream of air. (I) Option I: Electromagnet. Make an electromagnet and explore how to increase its strength.
